1. GPIOs 01

# Page 4^page=4
4 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems General Purpose Input/Outputs A GPIO is a configurable pin used to read or write digital signals. Modes: • Input → read external analog or digital signals (e.g., buttons, analog voltages…) • Output → drive analog or digital signals (e.g., LEDs, analog reference voltages…) • Alternate Function → used by peripherals (e.g., UART, SPI, Timers, etc.)

# Page 5^page=5
5 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems General Purpose Input/Outputs Register/logic side Input + output driver Pin side GPIOs: • 6 ports (A, …, E, H) • Each port 16 PINs

# Page 6^page=6
6 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems General Purpose Input/Outputs Pin protection and 5V tolerance • Two clamp diodes to V_DD and V_SS: ESD and overvoltage protection: They bound the voltage that can safely be applied to the pin. Internal pull-up/pull-down • Weak resistors (~30–50 kΩ), each with an independent on/off switch. • Options: floating, pull-up, pull- down (never both at once). • Use them for: floating lines, push-buttons, open-drain nets. • Prefer an external resistor when you need a precise value or more current.Pin side

# Page 7^page=7
7 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems General Purpose Input/Outputs Register/logic side Register/logic side • ODR: output data register (what the CPU writes) • IDR: input data register (what the CPU reads) • Read/Write/Read-Write buses link the cell to the core • Alternate-function path connects the pin to an on- chip peripheral • BSRR: atomic single-bit set/reset

# Page 8^page=8
8 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Alternate Functions

# Page 9^page=9
9 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems General Purpose Input/Outputs Input path and Schmitt trigger • Schmitt trigger with hysteresis: two thresholds, V_IL and V_IH • Purpose: noise immunity and clean edges from slow-rising inputs • IDR captures the digital level → Read bus • Alternate-function input feeds a peripheral (e.g. UART RX, timer capture) • Analog input bypasses the digital front-end and goes straight to the analog peripheral (ADC / comparator / DAC) Input driver

# Page 10^page=10
10 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems General Purpose Input/Outputs Output stage • MUX selects the source: ODR (general-purpose) or alternate-function output • Output control drives the two transistors • Push-pull: P-MOS + N-MOS actively drive both 0 and 1 • Open-drain: P-MOS off, only N-MOS → needs a pull-up (EX: I²C) • Disabled: both transistors off Output driver

# Page 11^page=11
11 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems General Purpose Input/Outputs Open-drain + pull-up • An open-drain stage can only pull the line low or release it. • It never drives high, so the pull-up is what creates the logic 1. • Example: I2C communication Input + pull • In input mode there is no output stage, so nothing fixes the pin level. • An unconnected input floats: it picks up noise, reads random 0/1, and can even draw extra current as the input buffer hovers around its threshold. The pull sets the resting level. • Example: Push-button to GND + internal pull-up

# Page 12^page=12
2. EXTI 02

# Page 13^page=13
13 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems General Purpose Input/Outputs As we discussed last time, each pin can be configured in the GUI. On some pins, there is an option named EXTI: what is it?

# Page 14^page=14
14 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems External interrupt (EXTI) peripheral • The EXTI (External Interrupt) on an STM32 microcontroller is a peripheral used to handle interrupts triggered by external events, such as changes in GPIO pins. • It allows specific pins to generate interrupts when they detect a rising edge, falling edge, or both. • Each EXTI line can be connected to a specific GPIO pin, and there are multiple EXTI lines available. • EXTI lines are connected to the NVIC, which manages the interrupt priorities and enables or disables them globally.

# Page 15^page=15
15 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems External interrupt (EXTI) peripheral EXTI can manage both interrupts and events: • When an interrupt occurs, the CPU is notified, and it immediately pauses its current execution to handle the interrupt by running an Interrupt Service Routine (ISR). After processing, it resumes its previous task. • An event can trigger specific actions in the system (e.g., starting a peripheral or changing internal states) without interrupting the CPU. Events are processed silently, allowing the CPU to continue its current execution unless explicitly handled by software.

# Page 16^page=16
16 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems External interrupt/event line mapping Up to 81 GPIOs (STM32F401xB/C and STM32F401xD/E) are connected to the 16 external interrupt/ event lines in the following manner. There are only 16 EXTI lines for GPIOs: line x connects to pin x of one selected port. The SYSCFG_EXTICR register picks which port. The five other EXTI lines are connected as follows: • EXTI line 16 is connected to the Power Voltage Detector (PVD) output • EXTI line 17 is connected to the Real Time Clock (RTC) Alarm event • EXTI line 18 is connected to the USB On-The-Go Full Speed (OTG FS) Wakeup event • EXTI line 21 is connected to the RTC Tamper and TimeStamp events • EXTI line 22 is connected to the RTC Wakeup event

# Page 17^page=17
17 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems SYSCFG Register map • The register map is the table listing, for each register, its address (offset) and what each bit does • Example: SYSCFG_EXTICR1 (offset 0x08) → bits [3:0] pick the port for EXTI0, [7:4] for EXTI1, … • Each EXTI line already knows its pin number, only the port must be chosen (PA0? PB0? PC0?) • Choosing 1 of up to 16 ports needs 4 bits (2⁴ = 16), even if specific MCUs have less (we have 6) • These 4 bits live in SYSCFG_EXTICRx: 0000 = port A, 0001 = B, …

# Page 18^page=18
18 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems EXTI block diagram Read the signal right → left: from Input line to CPU/hardware. Every wire is one structure, replicated for all 23 lines. • Edge detect circuit reacts to a change, not to a level • Rising edge: 0 → 1 • Falling edge: 1 → 0 • Set by the Rising / Falling trigger selection registers

# Page 19^page=19
19 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems EXTI block diagram After triggering, the signal splits into two paths: • Interrupt path → through the Interrupt mask register → Pending request register → out to the NVIC (runs the ISR) • Event path → through the Event mask register → Pulse generator (wakes the chip or starts another peripheral, no code) Each path has its own mask register → enable interrupt, event, both, or neither

# Page 20^page=20
20 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems EXTI block diagram Pending request register = a flag that stays on meaning "this line has a pending interrupt" It signals the NVIC, which stops the CPU and runs the ISR The flag must be cleared inside the ISR, otherwise the interrupt fires forever. It is cleared by writing 1 to it. The event path does not run code and does not set a pending flag. Through the Event mask register → Pulse generator → a short hardware pulse. Used to wake the chip from low-power mode or trigger another peripheral. Nothing to clear afterwards.

# Page 21^page=21
22 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems EXTI register map Mask registers (IMR / EMR) → enable interrupt / event per line. Trigger registers (RTSR / FTSR) → select rising / falling edge per line SWIER → trigger a line by software PR → pending flag (cleared by writing 1) Bits 0–15 = GPIO lines; bits 16–18 and 21-22 = internal lines (PVD, RTC, USB) Reset value = all 0 → nothing enabled at startup; you turn on only the bits you need

# Page 22^page=22
23 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Interrupt vector table • The vector table is an array of pointers located at a fixed memory address in the microcontroller (specifically in the code portion). • Each entry in the table is the starting address of an interrupt handler function (ISR). • When an interrupt occurs, the processor uses the vector table to jump to the corresponding ISR, executing the specific routine for that interrupt.

# Page 23^page=23
24 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Interrupt vector table Priority: p = n Priority: p ≥ n Priority: p = n Priority: p < n

# Page 26^page=26
27 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems GPIO HAL functions • Interrupts must be enabled in CUBE • All the interrupt routines are handled in stm32f4xx_it.c

# Page 27^page=27
28 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Project 1a: Pushbutton - polling • Objective of this project is to switch on the green LED on Nucleo board (LD2), every time the blue pushbutton is pressed and to switch it off when the pushbutton is released. • A polling operation will be used to monitor the state of the pushbutton.

# Page 28^page=28
29 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Project 1a hints • Use the NUCLEO board Manual to find the GPIO connected to the blue push-button and LD2. • Configure the GPIO in CUBE and generate the code. • In NUCLEO board Manual find the state of the blue button (0 or 1) when it is pressed. • Use the GPIO function the check the state of the push-button and consequently update the state of LD2. • Debug and verify if the LED is ON when you press it and OFF when you release it.

# Page 29^page=29
30 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Project 1b: Pushbutton - interrupt • Objective of this project is to switch on an LED every time the blue pushbutton is pressed, and to switch it off when the pushbutton is released. • The pushbutton input will be used in interrupt mode.

# Page 30^page=30
31 A. De Vecchi – Sensor Systems Project 1b hints • Configure CUBE, remembering to enable the interrupt for the pushbutton. Note that you need to modify the status of the LED both when you press and when you release the pushbutton. • Check in the stm32f4xx_it.c file that the routine which handles the EXTI from the pushbutton has been automatically prepared by CUBE. • Use the HAL_GPIO_EXTI_Callback to manage the interrupt (switch ON/OFF the LED), using the GPIO functions. • Debug and verify if the LED is ON when you press it and OFF when you release it. You should see the same behavior you had in the first project (polling), but now you are not using CPU resources just to wait for an event!
